doc.title: Von Freeman — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

chapter: Bird, Ben Webster and the 1950s decline
title: Navarro, McGhee and Diz; why the music declined
summary: Freeman says the bebop figures faded in the early 1950s and singers and rock and roll came in.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: Is jazz healthy? Young players, rock and the future

blocks.x: I know Fat Girl – what was his name? –
Fats Navarro. There’s another bad cat.
. . . he and Maggie, all those guys –
. . . yeah, Howard McGhee – all those guys were such a big part of the Chicago scene, because they were all coming to Chicago all the time. They almost all of them dissipated around the same time.
That’s true, all in the early ’50s.

So the music just said bip. Of course Diz, the warrior that he is, he tried to carry on with it, but Diz seemed to me like he went into his big band thing and then into Latin, a lot of Latin music and whatnot. Then he would get these different kind of bands that – where he was strictly the only star in the band. So when you went to hear him, and hear him . . .
Like what we were talking about.
Yeah, the same thing that we was talking about earlier. So the music just said, blah.
You think the bottom kind of dropped out.
Yeah, it sounded just – and during that time, the singers were coming out.
Plus you had the whole thing with Elvis Presley and all that starting to happen.
Yeah, all that started to happen.
The Chuck Berry thing was happening real early.
